message.content:
A CPU (Central Processing Unit) and a GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) are both processors, but they’re designed for different kinds of workloads:

| Feature | CPU | GPU |
|---------|-----|-----|
| **Primary purpose** | General‑purpose computing – handles everything from OS tasks to application logic. | Parallel graphics rendering – originally for rasterizing images, now also used for massively parallel compute tasks. |
| **Core count** | Few (2–32 in consumer CPUs, up to hundreds in server CPUs). | Hundreds to thousands of simpler cores. |
| **Core design** | Complex, high‑performance cores with deep pipelines, large caches, branch prediction, out‑of‑order execution. | Simple, lightweight cores optimized for throughput; each core does less work but many run simultaneously. |
| **Instruction set** | Rich, with many control‑flow instructions, SIMD extensions (e.g., AVX, SSE). | SIMD‑heavy, but each instruction operates on many data elements in lockstep. |
| **Memory hierarchy** | Large L1/L2/L3 caches per core, sophisticated memory controllers. | Smaller per‑core caches; relies on high‑bandwidth memory (HBM, GDDR) and shared memory spaces. |
| **Latency vs throughput** | Low latency – good for tasks that need quick responses or irregular branching. | High throughput – excels when the same operation is applied to many data items (e.g., matrix multiplication, image filtering). |
| **Typical workloads** | OS scheduling, database queries, web servers, general software. | Rendering 3D graphics, video encoding/decoding, scientific simulations, machine‑learning inference/training. |
| **Programming model** | Single‑threaded or multi‑threaded with complex synchronization. | Data‑parallel programming (CUDA, OpenCL, Vulkan compute, DirectCompute). |
| **Energy efficiency** | Optimized for performance per watt in a wide range of tasks. | Optimized for throughput per watt in highly parallel workloads. |

### Why the difference matters

- **Parallelism**: A GPU can launch thousands of threads that execute the same instruction on different data. A CPU can only launch a handful of threads that may run very different code paths.
- **Control flow**: CPUs handle divergent branches efficiently; GPUs suffer performance penalties when threads in the same warp diverge.
- **Memory access patterns**: GPUs thrive on coalesced memory accesses; CPUs benefit from cache locality.

In practice, modern systems use both: the CPU handles the “control” side of an application, while the GPU accelerates the “data‑parallel” side. This synergy is why GPUs have become popular for non‑graphics tasks like deep learning, scientific computing, and real‑time analytics.
